ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: m6A, or N6-methyladenosine, is the most abundant modification of mRNA transcripts. These modifications are known to influence mRNA transcript stability, transcription, translation, alternative splicing and decay, with undoubtedly more functions to be discovered. In this review, we explored the roles of m6A modifications in two groups of protozoan parasites: the apicomplexans, which include Plasmodium and Toxoplasma species, and kinetoplastids, which include Trypanosoma and Leishmania species. We also compared the key players of m6A epitranscriptomic machinery in creating, interpreting, and removing m6A modifications between these parasitic protists as well as a discussion of how m6A modifications facilitate parasite survival through features specific to apicomplexans and kinetoplastids. Beyond parasite epitranscriptomes, this review compares m6A dynamics in host and vector species (humans, flies and mosquitoes), highlighting coevolutionary adaptations. Strikingly, both the parasites and their vectors lack canonical m6A demethylases, implying a largely irreversible, streamlined m6A landscape fine-tuned for synchronized gene regulation. Overall, a mechanistic understanding is emerging of how m6A-modified RNAs and their binding proteins orchestrate RNA processing, translation, and turnover in parasitic protists, revealing an evolutionarily tuned epitranscriptomic system.

ce:section.ce:para: Epitranscriptomics seeks to understand how post-transcriptional chemical modifications made to RNA transcripts can modulate every aspect of the RNA life cycle [1,2]. RNA processing, transcript stability, structure, translation, localization and decay are all influenced by epitranscriptomic modifications [3]. More than 100 chemical post-transcriptional modifications contribute to modulation of RNA expression and the overall fate of RNA transcripts [4]. Among the most common chemical post-transcriptional modifications to RNA bases are pseudouridine (Ψ), 5-methylcytosine (m5C) and N6-methyladenosine (m6A), with m6A being the most abundant [3].

m6A is a reversible modification that occurs in a wide variety of RNAs: both mRNA and non-coding RNA transcripts experience m6A modifications [5]. m6A is installed co- or post-transcriptionally by a multicomponent "writer" complex, primarily consisting of METTL3 and METTL14, which methylates adenosine residues within a specific consensus motif (RRACH) [5]. Once deposited, m6A marks impact RNA metabolism by being recognized by "reader" proteins, such as those in the YTH domain family, which mediate downstream effects including splicing, nuclear export, translation, and decay [6]. These modifications are reversible, with "eraser" enzymes like FTO and ALKBH5 capable of demethylating m6A, thus allowing dynamic regulation in response to cellular conditions [6,7]. Unlike DNA epigenetic modifications, which involve covalent changes to the DNA molecule itself (e.g., cytosine methylation) and are primarily associated with long-term transcriptional silencing and heritable gene regulation, m6A RNA modifications act at the post-transcriptional level and provide a rapid, reversible mechanism to fine-tune gene expression without altering the underlying genetic code [8]. Unlike more static modifications such as pseudouridine or 2′-O-methylation, m6A is recognized by specific reader proteins that directly influence key aspects of RNA fate.

Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are essential molecular assemblies that coordinate the processing of RNA molecules in all domains of life. Within mRNA ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes, m6A modifications influence multiple aspects of mRNA metabolism, including splicing, export, localization, translation, and decay. As mentioned above, m6A regulation is primarily orchestrated by the coordinated actions of its writer and eraser proteins and from m6A recognition by m6A readers. Together, these m6A regulators modulate mRNP structure and function, orchestrating context-dependent post-transcriptional gene regulation. For instance, m6A reader protein YTHDF2 binding to m6A sites can recruit the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, leading to accelerated mRNA degradation [9]. Conversely, IGF2BP proteins (IGF2BP1-3) can bind m6A-modified mRNAs to enhance their stability and translation, demonstrating the context-dependent effects of m6A readers [10]. In addition, m6A modifications have been implicated in gene silencing as well [9]. m6A modification sites on XIST and retrotransposons play a key role in gene silencing by providing a binding site for YTHDC1, another m6A reader [9,11]. In all these examples, gene expression is modulated through the presence of m6A modification, leading to different outcomes for the modified transcripts. While they can occur anywhere in an RNA transcript, m6A modifications occur at higher frequencies near stop codons and the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR) [5,12,13]. In addition to m6A regulatory factors, such as writers, readers, and erasers being part of an active mRNP complex, how mRNA packaging could affect the accessibility of m6A in an mRNP complex during pre-RNA splicing, mRNA export and other processes such as mRNA folding and function remains a topic of active exploration [14–17].

In well-studied model organisms like Arabidopsis, Drosophila, C. elegans and mammalian systems, m6A epitranscriptomic regulation has been shown to control key processes such as development, stress responses, and cell fate decisions [18–20]. In contrast, parasitic protists remain largely understudied despite their complex life cycles and reliance on rapid gene expression changes for host adaptation, suggesting that investigating m6A and other RNA modifications in these organisms could reveal unique, evolutionarily divergent mechanisms of post-transcriptional regulation. In parasitic protozoans, epitranscriptomic control of factors influencing virulence and host immune evasion has become an active area of research due to the implications on human health and economies in areas where these parasites are endemic. Of particular interest are apicomplexan and kinetoplastid parasites [21]. These ancient parasites are deadly and relatively few preventative measures exist, leaving endemic communities vulnerable to widespread infection of both humans and livestock needed for subsistence and economic stability. In this review, we will examine the current status of the m6A epitranscriptomic research in parasitic protists, such as in Plasmodium, Toxoplasma (apicomplexan) and Trypanosoma (kinetoplastid) species, particularly focusing on the extent and mechanistic purview of m6A modifications of RNA in the RNP complexes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Genomic frameworks and regulatory mechanisms in apicomplexa and kinetoplastids
ce:section.ce:para: Among Apicomplexans (Plasmodium and Toxoplasma sp.), Plasmodium is a genus of unicellular, obligate intracellular parasitic protist that causes malaria [22]. It belongs to the apicomplexan phylum which is characterized by an apicoplast, an essential plastid endosymbiotically acquired from red algae chloroplasts [23]. Plasmodium species evade host immune responses through concealing themselves in host hepatocytes and erythrocytes [21]. The Plasmodium life cycle is complex; it is carried out in both sexual and asexual stages between an insect and a vertebrate host [21]. The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum is the deadliest amongst all the Plasmodium species infecting humans [21]. The life cycle of P. falciparum begins when an infected female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites into a human host during a blood meal [21]. These sporozoites travel to the liver, where they multiply and mature into merozoites that are released into the bloodstream to infect red blood cells, undergoing repeated asexual replication and causing the clinical symptoms of malaria [21]. During the intra-erythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) of P. falciparum, merozoites infecting human RBCs differentiate into three distinct life-stages: ring, trophozoite and schizonts, in about 48 ho [24]. Some merozoites differentiate into sexual forms called gametocytes, which are taken up by another mosquito where it completes the sexual cycle [25]. P. falciparum’s ∼23 Mb genome is extremely AT-rich and organized into 14 chromosomes encoding ∼5,300 genes. It features a high coding density and includes multigene families (var, rifin, and stevor genes for example) clustered in sub-telomeric regions that are important for antigenic variation [24,26]. Despite this complexity, P. falciparum lacks many canonical transcription factors and instead relies on a limited set of plant-like ApiAP2 transcription factors to orchestrate cascades of stage-specific transcription [27]. In addition, post-transcriptional regulations by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) [28] and RNA methylations [29–31] are prevalent, but their extent and mechanisms of functions are yet to be fully revealed.

Toxoplasma gondii, a well-characterized apicomplexan, causes toxoplasmosis in warm blooded animals, including humans, causing severe pathological impacts in immunodeficient patients and congenital cases [21]. Compared to P. falciparum, T. gondii possesses a larger genome (∼65 Mb, ∼8,300 genes, 13 chromosomes) with more balanced GC content. Both parasites share an Apicomplexan strategy of AP2-driven transcriptional control and chromatin-based regulation of developmental programs, but T. gondii’s expanded gene repertoire (e.g. ∼145 members of the SRS surface antigen family) and its flexible transcriptomic responses enable facultative life stage switching (tachyzoite–bradyzoite differentiation) in response to host cues [21,32,33].

Trypanosomatid parasites (Leishmania and Trypanosoma genera) are members of the kinetoplastid group, characterized by the kinetoplast [34]. Located in the mitochondrial matrix, the kinetoplast is a large network of interconnected DNA maxicircles encoding mitochondrial and ribosomal proteins, and minicircles encoding small guide RNAs to facilitate RNA editing [34,35]. These parasites complete their life cycles in two hosts: an insect vector (i.e. mosquitoes, sand flies, and tsetse flies) and a mammal such as humans or livestock [36]. They cause African sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis in human hosts and nagana in livestock [36]. To establish chronic infection in mammalian hosts, trypanosomatids must evade the host immune response [37]. Leishmania species exist as extracellular parasites in the sandfly vector and intracellular parasites in mammalian hosts and can get around the mammalian immune system through modulation of the complement response [38]. In Trypanosoma brucei, Variant Surface Glycoproteins (VSGs) that are expressed from sub-telomeric regions in the mammalian bloodstream coat the parasite [39]. When an immune response is mounted, the VSG coat is switched, which allows the parasite to evade immune recognition. The haploid genome of T. brucei is 26–35 Mb in size, depending on the strain, encoding around 9,000 genes. Unlike typical eukaryotes, T. brucei transcribes its protein-coding genes as long polycistronic transcription units, which are subsequently processed into individual mRNAs by trans-splicing and polyadenylation. Post-transcriptional regulation in kinetoplastids occurs mainly through mRNA stability, translation efficiency, and localization, governed by stage-specific RNA-binding proteins, cis-regulatory elements in untranslated regions (UTRs), and RNA modifications such as m6A [21,40–42]. This allows rapid and flexible responses to environmental changes during complex life cycles in both the insect vector and mammalian host.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Modifying the message: An introduction to m6A RNA epigenetics
ce:section.ce:para: m6A is the most common epitranscriptomic modification found in eukaryotic organisms, affecting approximately 30 % of transcripts [43]. This modification can be added to or removed from RNA transcripts to meet the changing needs of the cell [4,9,43]. The m6A modifications are made by methyltransferases (writers), recognized by RNA-binding proteins (readers), and removed by demethylases (erasers) [44]. The activity of these proteins is dynamic and changes in response to intracellular and extracellular stimuli [44].

Methyltransferases known as “writers” install the m6A modifications on RNA transcripts [44]. The complex of methyltransferase-like 3 and methyltransferase-like 14 (METTL3-METTL14) is the known writer for m6A modifications [44]. In the METTL3-METTL14 complex, METTL3 is the catalytically active component because it is an S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) binding protein and can methylate an adenine in a target RNA containing the consensus motif RRACH (where R is adenine or guanine, A is adenine, C is cytosine, and H is adenine, cytosine or uracil) [45,46]. METTL14, on the other hand is not a SAM binding protein, but it facilitates m6A modification deposition by binding to the RNA sequences and stabilizing them, then dimerizing with METTL3[43,44,47]. The METTL3 component actually deposits the m6A modification [47]. Apart from each other, the methyltransferase activity of METTL3 and METTL14 is relatively low, but when they form a complex, the activity is significantly increased [47].The METTL3-METTL14 complex interacts with Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP), which is not catalytically active, but it does play a crucial role in complex localization [48].

Once an m6A modification has been made, its effect is directed by RNA-binding proteins that recognize m6A modifications on target RNA transcripts, known as “readers” [44,49]. Reader proteins can change how the pre-mRNA is processed into a mature transcript and where it is localized [50]. Reader proteins may work either directly or indirectly [44]. YT521-B family proteins are direct reader proteins united by their common YTH m6A binding domain [5,44,51]. The members of the YTH domain family (YTHDF) cause different responses in the m6A modifications they bind [43]. The reader proteins YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3, and YTHDC2 are all localized to the cytoplasm, but they have different functions. The YTHDF1 and YTHDF3 increases translation, while YTHDF2 aids in the facilitation of mRNA decay [5]. YTHDC2 is implicated in the recruitment of RNA binding proteins that modulate translation and transcript degradation [52]. Indirect readers require the assistance of an m6A switch to locate m6A modifications and subsequently change the RNA conformation to ease protein binding [53].

“Eraser” demethylases remove m6A modifications from RNA transcripts through oxidative demethylation [44]. Fat mass and obesity associated protein (FTO) was the first to be discovered and has been demonstrated to be an eraser of m6A modifications [7,44]. In addition to reversing m6A modifications, FTO demethylates N6,2-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) modifications with a preference for the m6Am modifications near the 5’ cap and N1-methyladenosine (m1A) in tRNAs, impacting translation [54,55]. FTO has no known consensus motif and is recruited to demethylate RNA transcripts in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm [6].

Alkb homolog 5 (ALKBH5) is the second known m6A eraser demethylase [44,56]. This eraser is localized to the nucleus and m6A modifications are its sole substrate [44,56]. ALKBH5 has demonstrated a capacity to modulate RNA export from the nucleus as well as other RNA metabolic processes [44,56].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Tools and techniques for mapping m6A in RNA-protein assemblies
ce:section.ce:para: In the context of RNP and mRNP complexes, detection of m6A modifications can be achieved via antibody-based assays, advanced sequencing methods, and mass spectrometry, each with distinct trade-offs. Antibody-based approaches such as MeRIP-seq (methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing) use anti-m6A antibodies to enrich methylated RNA fragments for high-throughput sequencing, enabling transcriptome-wide identification of m6A-modified regions but only at ∼100–200-nucleotide resolution [13]. Immunoprecipitation-based m6A modification detection techniques are not the most efficient way to identify m6A modifications in RNA transcripts [21]. These assays require a large amount of input material, which could be difficult to obtain given the lack of specificity found in most m6A detection antibodies [21]. Mass spectrometry (typically LC–MS/MS analysis of nucleosides from hydrolyzed RNA) provides a chemically definitive and quantitative readout of m6A in RNA samples, including RNP-associated RNAs, allowing accurate determination of overall m6A levels and modification stoichiometry. However, MS-based approaches do not inherently reveal the nucleotide sequence context or exact sites of modification and thus lack the spatial resolution of sequencing-based methods. In contrast, enzyme- or chemical-based mapping techniques (e.g. MAZTER-seq and DART-seq) leverage m6A-sensitive reactions to introduce identifiable sequence changes at m6A positions. For instance, selective RNase cleavage blocked by m6A at a specific motif, or a directed C to U conversion adjacent to m6A (assuming that the m6A methylation happens in the canonical RRACH motif) via an APOBEC1-YTH fusion enzyme, thereby achieving single-base precision and high specificity without antibody enrichment, at the cost of being constrained to certain sequence contexts or requiring engineered enzymatic tools [57,58]. Importantly, DART-seq can be used to determine in-cell epitranscriptomic signatures [58]. Most recently, direct RNA sequencing via Nanopore technology can detect m6A in native RNA strands by measuring altered electrical current signals at modified bases, reaching base-level resolution while surveying full-length RNAs [59,60]. Many of the above technologies are now being used to map m6A sites in the Apicomplexan and Kinetoplastid transcriptomes [29,61–66], which are described below.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cross-kingdom code: m6A signatures in hosts and vectors of parasitic protists
ce:section.ce:para: Recent studies have begun to elucidate the role of host mRNA methylation machinery during parasitic infections, revealing parasite-induced alterations that may impact post-transcriptional gene regulation in host species [67,68]. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification is largely orchestrated by a conserved set of enzymes across mammals (human, mouse, cat, cattle), although subtle species-specific differences exist. All four species harbor orthologous m6A “writer” proteins, most notably the METTL3–METTL14 methyltransferase complex along with the adapter WTAP and other co-factors (e.g. KIAA1429/VIRMA, RBM15, ZC3H13) that together form the core m6A writer complex, as described in an earlier section. Likewise, the m6A “readers” are well conserved: humans, mice, cats, and cattle, which are the definitive hosts for all the parasitic species described here (Plasmodium falciparum: primarily humans, Toxoplasma gondii: felines/wild cats, Trypanosoma brucei: humans, cattle, and Leishmania: humans and animals), possess the YTH domain-containing reader proteins (cytoplasmic YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3 and nuclear YTHDC1, YTHDC2) which recognize m6A containing transcripts via a homologous YTH RNA-binding domain to regulate mRNA splicing, stability, and translation. The m6A “erasers”, the demethylases FTO and ALKBH5, are also present in all these species, enabling reversible RNA methylation. Overall, gene ortholog and functional studies indicate that the composition and roles of m6A machinery are broadly similar in the mammalian hosts of these parasites and disruption of METTL3/METTL14 or key readers (e.g. YTHDF2, YTHDC2) leads to developmental or fertility defects, mirroring the importance of these factors across species [69,70]. Variations in m6A depositions and component functions across mammalian system and other organisms could be guided by changes in m6A consensus motifs and RNA secondary structures [71,72]. Core m6A regulators in mammalian hosts and their respective parasite species are depicted in [Figure-1].

Insect genomes, representing several disease vectors such as Anopheles, tsetse flies, and sand flies which spread malaria, Trypanosomiasis, and Leishmaniasis respectively, also contain conserved components of m6A regulatory proteins, sharing homology with model insects, such as Drosophila melanogaster [19]. Drosophila also has orthologs of accessory writer components like KIAA1429/VIRMA (fly Virilizer) and RBM15 (fly Spenito, aka Nito), all of which integrate into the m6A writer complex [73]. These writer components are not unique to Drosophila; genomic surveys show that Anopheles mosquitoes likewise possess the full toolkit of METTL3/METTL14, WTAP, etc., with similar domain structures [74]. Insect genomes also encode “reader” proteins with YTH domains that bind m6A marks. Notably, flies and mosquitoes appear to have a simplified YTH family compared to mammals: Drosophila has a single nuclear YTHDC1 ortholog and a single cytoplasmic YTHDF ortholog. Similarly, the yellow-fever mosquito vector Aedes aegypti genome contains at least one YTHDF-like reader (identified as the homolog of human YTHDF3) and one YTHDC1, rather than the multiple paralogs found in vertebrates. Anopheles species mosquitoes contain potential m6A readers, such as HAKAI, RBM15 and VIRMA, and YTHDC and YTHDF [74]. [Figure-1] also lists the canonical m6A factors present in insect species. Finally, insect genomes lack canonical demethylases as FTO and ALKBH5 are absent or not apparent in insects. Instead, another ALKBH family enzyme (likely ALKBH8) has been proposed as a putative m6A demethylase in insects [75,76].

Thus, emerging evidence indicates that parasitic infections reshape the host’s RNA methylome [67,68]. These alterations may involve shifts in global m6A abundance, redistribution of modification sites, and modulation of the expression or activity of m6A writer, reader, and eraser proteins [67]. For example, infections with malaria parasites such as Plasmodium yoelii induce substantial changes in the m6A methylome of the host spleen, impacting both the overall levels of m6A modification and the specific transcripts that are modified. In this case, four P. yoelii strains were used to infect mouse models to analyze m6A levels in spleen and blood mRNA. The levels of m6A modifications varied in each strain [67]. MeRIP-seq analysis revealed that 80 % of m6A peaks were unique to infected spleen samples, while the other 20 % of m6A peaks overlapped with noninfected control samples [67]. Further, the RRACH motif was enriched for m6A peaks, with increased levels in the 5′UTR and CDS in P. yoelli infected samples [67]. Looking into interferon pathway-related genes, m6A peaks and expression were upregulated in infected samples, indicating their potential role in the host’s immune response [67]. This evidence highlights the significance of m6A methylation in the intricate interaction between host and pathogen, impacting the parasite's lifecycle.

ce:section.ce:section-title: m6A signatures and regulators in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma parasites
ce:section.ce:para: In Plasmodium species, there is growing evidence to confirm the presence of m6A modifications. With the modification being conserved in eukaryotes, writer and reader proteins specific to Plasmodium species have recently been uncovered. Writer proteins MT-A70 (PF3D7_0729500), MT-A70.2 (PF3D7_1235500), and WTAP (PF3D7_1230800) are homologs of the conserved methyltransferase proteins, whereas PfMT-A70 has been identified as the ortholog of METTL3 [29]. Similarly, proteins containing an m6A reader ‘YTH’ domain have been characterized as Plasmodium reader proteins: PfYTH1 (PF3D7_1419900) and PfYTH2 (PF3D7_0309800) [30,77] [Table 1]. The YTH domain forms a cage-like structure around the methyl group of m6A, having interactions with nucleotides before and after the modification. Previous studies have indicated that this binding has weak affinity, suggesting the need for additional interactors to form a stable bound complex [49]. Interestingly, PfYTH1 was shown to be highly expressed during intraerythrocytic development (IDC), while PfYTH2 expression was highest during the parasite’s transmission stages [30,77]. Differential expression of these proteins during the Plasmodium life cycle suggests that they may be gene specific. Intriguingly, PfYTH1 is a homolog of plant (Arabidopsis) polyadenylation and cleavage factor subunit CPSF30-L [78,79]. Additionally, PfYTH2 localizes to the cytoplasm, whereas PfYTH1 is suggested to localize to the nucleus due to its similarities to CPSF30 [79]. [Fig. 2] shows stage specific expression of the m6A readers as well as ubiquitous expression of the writer proteins in the intraerythrocytic asexual cycles of P. falciparum.

In comparison to other organisms, Plasmodium species contain higher levels of m6A modifications, where it has been shown to be involved in processes such as the regulation of translational plasticity [79]. m6A has been implicated in mRNA stability in addition to translation efficiency (TE). PfYTH2 preferentially binds to the 3′UTR of many genes, further suggesting the enrichment of m6A in these regions [30,79] and its direct implication in translational control is currently being determined [81]. Through co-immunoprecipitation and LC-MS, PfYTH2 was found to interact with proteins coupled with translational machinery: two polyadenylate binding-like proteins, three proteasomal proteins involved in degradation processes, and three subunits of eIF3 [77], a large multi-subunit complex that plays a critical role in translation initiation in eukaryotes. Following this, work was done to uncover PfYTH2’s impact on TE. Conditional technology, knock-sideways of PfYTH2, revealed an increase in TE across all genes included in the study, with peaks between 24 and 26 hp77. TE and m6A density appeared to be independent of one another, but increases in TE did occur in genes with higher m6A density [77]. To identify the involvement of PfYTH2 in P. falciparum’s IDC, changes in parasitemia were measured in PfYTH2-sandwich and PfYTH2-sandwichML in the presence and absence of rapamycin, a drug that has shown to suppress certain malarial strains [77]. The PfYTH2-sandwich was created by flanking GFP on either side by FK506 binding protein domains to the C-terminus of PfYTH2 copy, while the PfYTH2-sandwichML was created by transfecting PfYTH2-sandwich parasites with a plasmid containing a cell membrane mislocalizer [77]. Parasites had the highest parasitemia in the absence of RAP, but the PfYTH2-sandwichML parasites showed a significant decrease when exposed to RAP, suggesting that the mislocalization of PfYTH2 has some impact on parasitic replication and survival [77].

Mapping of m6A in the context of cell-extracted RNA or RNAs isolated from RNP complexes have been performed through techniques such as DART-seq and MeRIP-seq respectively to globally map m6A sites at single-nucleotide resolution within the P. falciparum genome. Not only was m6A prevalent near the 3′ end of the coding region, but overlap of m6A sites identified by DART-seq was within the consensus RAC motif [65]. The proximity of the modifications to the 3′UTR suggests their potential role in mRNA 3′-end processing events, such as polyadenylation or alternative polyadenylation. DART-seq aided in the discovery of stage-specific gene regulation by m6A. Plasmodium parasites tightly regulate their gene expression through asexual development. Unique and shared m6A sites have been identified across the ring, trophozoite, and schizont stages. Strikingly, several genes involved in stress responses such as heat-shock or artemisinin resistance presented with upregulated levels of m6A [65]. This paired with the decreased susceptibility of the parasites to artemisinin-like therapies suggests a critical gene regulatory role of m6A in malaria biology.

Like Plasmodium species, additional evidence continues to show that other apicomplexan parasites, like Toxoplasma, contain m6A modifications. The writer complex has been shown to contain the conserved mammalian proteins METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP [62]. Using HA epitope tagging, each of these writer proteins subsequently tagged to observe their localization. Each protein localized in the parasite nuclei, but interestingly, METTL14 (TGME49_268840) expression was greatly diminished compared to both METTL3 (TGME49_217350) and WTAP (TGME49_212960) [62]. Further validation of the core writer complex’s interactions was done through immunoprecipitation, where METTL14 and METLL3 were consistently pulled down together, with WTAP peptides occasionally being pulled down. WTAP instead was found to have a strong association to TGGT1_275990 and TGGT1_226660, where TGGT1_275990 is unique to coccidian parasites and TGGT1_226660 is homologous to the N-terminal domain of VIRMA [62,64]. This suggests that these proteins are exclusive to specific apicomplexans [Figure-1] and may be involved in guiding the m6A writer complex to the 3′UTR [62]. Depletion of the core writer complex led to a drastic decrease in m6A levels and parasite viability. Interestingly, two contradicting motifs were identified across different T. gondii strains. DDAC (where D is adenine, uracil, or guanine), a sequence like the m6A consensus sequence RRACH, was common in many of the studied strains, while the YGCAUGCR was discovered in others through different studies [62,64].

In addition to characterizing the writer complex, m6A reader proteins containing the YTH domain were also found in Toxoplasma. Proteins of the gene IDs TGGT1_201200 (YTH1) and TGGT1_204070 (YTH2) were both shown to localize to the nucleus and were detected through Western blot analysis. Through immunoprecipitation to investigate their function, YTH1 co-purified with proteins involved in polyadenylation and 3′ cleavage, sharing a protein domain with the plant protein cleavage and polyadenylation specialty factor 30, long form (CPSF30-L) [62]. YTH2 also shares homology with CPSF30, but its associated proteins include a member of the 3′-end cleavage factor I complex and another that is homologous to the N-terminal of Rb-binding protein 6 in mammals (RBBP6) [62]. This reveals that the YTH proteins are involved in polyadenylation machinery and 3′-end cleavage. [Figure-3] shows structural homology of the apicomplexan ‘YTH’ domain containing reader proteins in apicomplexan parasites with plant CPSF30. It is important to note that m6A erasers have yet to be identified in apicomplexans [82].

The distribution of m6A methylation across three strains of T. gondii tachyzoites (ME49, RH, and VEG) showed enrichment in the 3′UTR [64]. It was discovered that methylation occurred in 2/3 of tachyzoite genes, indicating the role of m6A as an epigenetic marker. MeTPeak detected 1,896 peaks in a tachyzoite data set across 866 genes and 1,841 peaks within 687 genes from early bradyzoites [62]. Despite these findings, there is a need for m6A mapping throughout the parasite’s life cycle, as most work has been done in tachyzoites. Addressing the functional implications of m6A during stage conversion due to stress has not yet been fully explored.

ce:section.ce:section-title: m6A signatures and regulators in Trypanosoma parasites
ce:section.ce:para: m6A modifications have been identified in Trypanosoma parasites [41,80]. While METTL3-METTL14 in complex with WTAP form the methyltransferase writer complex in mammals, and is conserved in many other eukaryotes, no orthologous complex has been identified in trypanosomatids, likely because the sequences are much different from more recently-branched eukaryotes [41,83]. In trypanosomes, YTH-domain containing proteins have not yet been identified [80]. However, proteins with RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) have been established as RNA-interacting proteins [Figure-1] and may modulate gene expression through post-transcriptional interactions [84,85]. One such RRM-domain containing protein, TRRM2 [Table-1], has been identified as a potential reader of m6A modifications [80]. This difference may be a result of changed protein sequences through evolutionary time as mammals branched much later than trypanosomes [41]. To date, no erasers have been identified in trypanosomatids, which calls into question how m6A modifications are reversed (if at all) in these parasites [83].

The m6A modifications found in Trypanosoma species were identified through an immunoprecipitation-based approach that purified RNA transcripts with m6A modifications [80]. While immunoprecipitation has long been the gold standard for identifying m6A modifications, it comes with drawbacks, namely in non-specific binding and low sensitivity of the antibody in further analyses. More recently, methods such as antibody-free DART-seq and antibody- and amplification-free direct RNA sequencing on the Oxford Nanopore platform are available for identifying m6A modifications in Trypanosoma parasites [58]. The Nanopore-based methods are particularly attractive for their ease of handling and reduced amount of necessary input materials, which makes the assay more sustainable for long-term studies [86].

Gene expression in kinetoplastids, such as Trypanosoma brucei, is primarily regulated post-transcriptionally, making them unique among eukaryotes [87,88]. These organisms represent a unique clade among early eukaryotes as they exhibit extraordinary features of RNA metabolism, such as trans-splicing, polycistronic transcription and RNA editing [89,90] as novel features of RNA processing. Among the RNA intrinsic features, T. brucei was demonstrated to harbor m6A modifications and showed evidence that the modification was enriched in the 3′ poly(A) tails of transcripts [63,91]. The significance of the m6A modification enrichment in and near the transcript 3′ poly(A) tails is quite pronounced in the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) coding genes as half of the signatures found in the VSG transcripts were in poly(A) tails [91]. The VSGs are a crucial element of T. brucei immune response evasion, which contributes to the overall virulence and survival of the parasite [39]. The enrichment of m6A modifications in the 3′-poly(A) tails of the VSG genes was implicated in stabilizing the transcripts, which prevented their rapid degradation, promoting parasite survival [91].

The presence of m6A modifications in Trypanosoma parasites raised an important question: How, if at all, do m6A modifications vary between different life cycle stages of these parasites? Trypanosoma parasites have dual-host life cycles which are completed in the insect vector and a mammalian reservoir host [21]. The two hosts present the parasites with vastly different living conditions. Differences in body temperature, nutrient source and immune responses would likely be connected to differential levels of m6A modification between life cycle stages. Work published in 2019 by Liu and colleagues provided evidence of stage-specific differences in m6A modifications in Trypanosoma brucei, which they hypothesized had a regulatory impact on the RNA transcripts [80]. m6A modifications were identified in both T. brucei life cycle stages, and they occurred at the CUA consensus motif, which was different from the eukaryotic consensus sequence, RRACH [60,80].

m6A modifications were more abundant in the procyclic form (insect midgut) than in the bloodstream form (mammalian bloodstream) [80]. The much higher prevalence of m6A modifications in the procyclic form indicates that there may a stage-specific function of the modifications [80]. The modifications themselves experienced different distribution patterns in the bloodstream form and procyclic form cells-there was an approximately equal distribution of m6A modifications in the 5′-UTR, coding sequences and 3′-UTR of bloodstream form cells while there was a markedly higher amount of m6A modifications in the coding sequences than the 5′-UTR or 3′-UTR of procyclic form cells [80]. The higher incidence of m6A modifications in procyclic form coding sequences may indicate a role in modulating gene expression in a manner that is not necessary for parasite survival in the bloodstream form cells.

The next big question addresses how m6A modifications change from one parasitic life cycle stage to the next. T. brucei has varied needs between life cycle stages and changes to m6A modifications are expected to change with those needs. Serra et al. studied the m6A modification patterns across three developmental stages (slender, stumpy and procyclic) in which two stages (slender and procyclic) were proliferative and stumpy was quiescent [63]. Immunoprecipitated RNA went through the standard Pico Nextera library preparation before sequencing with the Illumina NextSeq 550 [63]. Modified transcripts were aligned and identified through SAMtools and StringTie before the enrichment of m6A modifications was calculated using R statistical software programs [63]. They learned that only 21 % of modified transcripts were conserved between all three developmental stages, suggesting that the m6A methylation patterns varied widely throughout the parasite’s life cycle [63]. Additionally, there was a higher level of m6A modification in the non-proliferative stumpy form and 47 % of the unique m6A modified transcripts were found in this proliferative stage [63]. The high prevalence of these modifications in the stumpy form indicate a possible role for m6A modifications in getting the parasite ready for transmission to its tsetse fly insect vector [63]. Furthermore, many of the modified stumpy form transcripts were implicated in RNA metabolism as m6A modifications in these transcripts could be the cause of diminished translation [63]. Serra and colleagues demonstrated that the procyclin surface proteins of the procyclic form were not affected by m6A modifications and that not all variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) mRNA transcripts undergo demethylation when they transition from stumpy to slender forms in the bloodstream [63]. This finding follows the discovery of m6A modifications in the VSGs which could regulate the parasite’s ability to evade the host immune response [91].

Although specific RNA-binding proteins are responsible for depositing and recognizing m6A marks, these modifications can also influence how other RNA-binding proteins interact with RNA transcripts. The deposition of m6A modifications on RNA transcripts can change the stability and structure of the modified transcript, thus changing the binding dynamics for other RNA binding proteins [92]. The m6A-switch is a structural mechanism that relies on m6A modification-driven changes to the RNA transcript’s structure that alter the accessibility of different RNA molecule domains [92,93]. These m6A-switch-induced structural changes modulate the transcript’s accessibility to RNA binding proteins, which influence the overall fate of the transcript [92]. Both mRNAs and long non-coding RNAs were examined and it was observed that m6A modifications adjust the local RNA structure to promote interaction between modified transcripts and heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C to stimulate RNA processing [92].

While the m6A-switch has not been identified in Trypanosoma parasites, the presence of m6A modifications can alter the ability of other RNA-binding proteins to associate with modified transcripts, which is consequential for RNA stability [91]. A simple example of this phenomenon has been observed in the m6A modified VSG transcripts [91]. When m6A modifications are present in the 3′-poly(A) tail of the VSG transcripts, those transcripts are shielded from the formation of a ribonucleoprotein between the modified transcript and proteins promoting deadenylation [91]. Through blocking RNA-binding proteins responsible for deadenylation, the RNA transcript is stabilized, which promotes translation into the VSGs that aid the parasite in evading the immune system [91]. While m6A modifications are known to directly impact RNA fate, they are also quite capable of indirectly changing the way RNA transcripts are processed, translated, or degraded.

m6A modifications play intricate regulatory roles in apicomplexan and kinetoplastid protozoan parasites. In both groups, m6A modifications are enriched at or near the 3’ end of RNA transcripts, especially trypanosomes, contain m6A marks in their mRNA poly(A) tails [65,91]. Because polyadenylation is one of the basic post-transcriptional modifications that directly influences the fate of the transcript, the presence of m6A modifications in this region suggests that the modification may be directly involved in processing mRNA transcripts so that they can be translated into functional proteins. Furthermore, the m6A modification rates between parasitic developmental stages suggest that the m6A modifications have an impact on life cycle stage-specific gene expression as well as transitions between life cycle stages [67]. In addition to contributing to high-level mRNA processing and developmental transitions, m6A modifications have the ability to modulate RNA transcript stability in both groups of protozoan parasites, which is a mechanism the parasites use to promote or repress gene expression to meet the cellular needs [9]. When considered together, these points of evidence show that the m6A modifications may influence gene expression and protein translation in similar ways between different groups of parasites.

Between protozoan parasites, the outcome of an m6A modification could have very different impacts. In Trypanosoma parasites, the presence of m6A modifications has demonstrated transcript stabilizing effects and prevents the degradation of modified transcripts. This is of significance in the RNA transcripts encoding variant surface glycoproteins, which protect the modified transcripts from degradation and support the parasite’s evasion of host immune responses [91]. However, the opposite has been observed in Plasmodium species - the incorporation of m6A modifications leads to an overall decrease in transcript stability and efficiency of translation [29]. As expected, the different needs of each parasite contribute significantly to this divergence in outcome from the same modification. The stabilizing impact of m6A modifications is closely associated with the need for extracellular parasites to evade the mammalian host immune response to facilitate chronic infection and survival. For intracellular Plasmodium parasites, a large part of the immune evasion is derived from “hiding out” inside host cells, therefore, there isn’t as great of a need for the parasite to use m6A modifications to mask itself from immune neutralization. In fact, a destabilization of m6A modified transcripts can facilitate the degradation of transcripts that have served their purposes and are not needed at the parasite’s specific developmental state.

Epitranscriptomic modifications are implicated in regulating a wide variety of biological processes. When the modifications are dysregulated, disease is a common outcome [43]. Furthermore, abnormal deposition, interpretation and removal of m6A modifications have demonstrated an association with poor outcomes for patients as they are involved in disease progression (e.g. metastasis and drug resistance) [94]. In mammals, METTL3, which deposits m6A modifications, YTH domain family proteins that interpret the modifications, and the FTO protein that removes them are all implicated in the development of cancerous tumors and provide researchers with several different potential drug development targets [94]. The ubiquitous nature of m6A modifications is mirrored in the ways that they can influence disease development and therefore, how the affected pathways can be therapeutically targeted [94].

While both Plasmodium and Trypanosoma species are protozoan parasites, the ways in which m6A modifications are written, read and erased have some variability. In Plasmodium species, the writers and readers are conserved homologs of METTL3/METTL14/WTAP found in other eukaryotes [62,64]. Like Caenorhabditis elegans and Dictyostelium discoideum, Trypanosoma parasites have no known writers [95]. The presence of m6A modifications is evidence that there must be a writer, but homology searches have returned no conserved writers yet. Researchers must continue the search for the elusive m6A writer in Trypanosoma species, with the understanding that the parasite’s early divergence could mean that the ancestral writers do not share much similarity with later branching eukaryotes with known writers [41,80,83]. This difference between the parasite groups is highlighted again in the readers. While Plasmodium readers have YTH domains, the single Trypanosoma reader does not [41,80,83]. It is possible that RNA recognition motifs are an ancestral trait and that YTH domains evolved later. Finally, neither group of parasitic protozoans have known erasers [21,82]. The absence of identified eraser demethylase proteins implies that m6A modifications may be reversed by non-canonical erasers, if they are reversible in Plasmodium and Trypanosoma parasites [21,82].

In the absence of demethylases, which serve as erasers to discretely remove the m6A modifications in RNA and since P. falciparum mRNA coding regions are hypermethylated by m6A methyltransferases, it is plausible that the m6A reader P. falciparum CPSF30, plays a potentially rate limiting step in selectively regulating m6A in a transcript-specific manner, for gene regulation. The CPSF proteins are polyadenylation cleavage and specificity factors found in eukaryotes that process pre-mRNA transcripts [96]. Some of these proteins have their own m6A reader domains and are closely associated with m6A modifications implicated in 3′ end processing, which directly impacts the organism’s ability to stop transcription [21,82]. CPSF30/CPSF4 is a YTH domain-containing reader protein found in plants that shares similarities with the Plasmodium (PfYTH1) and Toxoplasma reader proteins [Figure-3]. In the plants it is commonly found in, CPSF30 is a driver of alternative polyadenylation, which creates many different RNA isoforms that can produce different proteins [78]. Therapeutic targeting of CPSF30 (and its similar Plasmodium protein PfYTH1) could modulate the transcripts available for translation into functional proteins, which may impact disease prognosis and progression.

In P. falciparum, where no confirmed demethylase has been identified, YTH-domain-containing reader proteins such as PfYTH2 have been shown to bind m6A-marked transcripts and modulate their translational fate, acting as translational repressors that associate with mRNP complexes. Similarly, in T. brucei, which also lacks canonical erasers, non-YTH m6A-binding proteins like TRRM2 may functionally compensate by recruiting downstream effectors to methylated transcripts. These findings suggest that selective m6A reader-mediated regulation provides a stable, tunable mechanism for controlling gene expression in organisms with limited epitranscriptomic plasticity. The fact that both Plasmodium parasites and their Anopheles mosquito vectors lack canonical m6A demethylases (such as FTO/ALKBH5) suggests a convergent streamlining of the m6A machinery that may have coevolutionary advantages. In a co-adapted life cycle, this simplified m6A system, with methylation “writers” and binding “readers” but no active erasers, could ensure that methylation marks on mRNAs are stably maintained, yielding predictable gene expression outcomes synchronized between parasite and vector. Such coordination echoes other Plasmodium and Anopheles coevolutionary processes. For example, malaria parasites have evolved immune evasion strategies tightly coupled to mosquito immunity [97]. Likewise, metabolic interdependence underscores their coevolution: a notable example is the mosquito-derived metabolite xanthurenic acid, which the parasite has adapted to sense as a cue for gamete formation upon ingestion by the mosquito, linking Plasmodium sexual development to the vector’s physiology [98]. Taken together, these parallels support the idea that Plasmodium and Anopheles may have co-adapted their regulatory systems ranging from immune signaling and metabolism to chromatin and epitranscriptomic control, in a way that optimizes their intertwined life cycles.

m6A modifications in protozoan parasites have demonstrated their capacity to fine-tune parasite cellular processes. Their installation and interpretation machinery provide intriguing avenues for therapeutic development. m6A modifications require the coordinated actions of writers, readers and erasers to modulate an organism’s gene expression program. Among these three, the most attractive therapeutic target comes from the studies of reader proteins in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma apicomplexan parasites, which are homologs of the plant protein, CPSF30. The apicomplexan reader proteins PfYTH1 (P. falciparum) and YTH1 (T. gondii) exhibit some shared homology with CPSF30 in Arabidopsis thaliana, which typically harbors a a YTH domain-connecting mRNA polyadenylation and m6A modification [78,82]. CPSF30 is a key protein involved in the polyadenylation process, specifically in the recognition of the polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA) in pre-mRNA and its homologs in apicomplexan parasites intuitively may play a role in pre-mRNA 3′-end processing mediated by m6A modifications [82]. The inhibition of CPSF protein complexes implicated in pre-mRNA end processing, including alternative polyadenylation, has become a target for therapeutic development to modulate the levels of mature mRNA transcripts [82]. A less understood reader protein in P. falciparum, PfYTH2, has been named as an essential protein for parasitic growth through ligand-inducible relocalization (knock-sideways), where PfYTH1 was unable to compensate for the loss of its function [77]. PfYTH2 has been shown to interact with translational machinery, which may be of interest as a potential drug target as further studies are carried out to confirm its functionality in translational processes. Even though m6A writers have not been definitively identified in kinetoplastids, benzoxaboroles, which can act on CPSF proteins involved in pre-mRNA 3′-end processing, have shown some efficacy against Leishmania and Trypanosoma parasites [82]. Additionally, the compound AN3661 can diminish parasitic replication in apicomplexans through binding zinc atoms in CPSF3 [82,99]. Investigations of pre-mRNA 3′-end processing inhibitors do raise some serious safety concerns such as how inhibitors impact mRNA metabolism [82]. Furthermore, drug resistance, off-target binding and unintentional interference in the host organism’s m6A machinery are critical issues that must be fully explored in the research and development pipeline to ensure patient safety.

Amongst the writer proteins, METTL3 has come to the forefront as a possible therapeutic target. Currently, a METTL3 ortholog has not been identified in Trypanosoma brucei through sequence homology search or other means. The lack of a known ortholog is not definitive evidence that another class of writer protein is depositing m6A modifications in T. brucei, but it does suggest that the well-characterized METTL3-METTL14-WTAP writer complex evolved from a precursor that may be found in ancient parasites such as T. brucei. In P. falciparum, CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown of the METTL3 ortholog PfMT-A70 during the intra-erythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) caused a 10–30 % transcriptome-wide decrease in m6A modifications, which was correlated with increased mRNA transcript stability and translation efficiency [29]. While the knockdown of PfMT-A70 does not interfere with parasitic growth, these results indicate that the modulation a critical component of the m6A writer complex in P. falciparum generates changes to the transcriptome and resultant proteome throughout the IDC, which is responsible for malaria symptoms in humans [29]. The challenge in targeting P. falciparum is identifying the most effective agent for knockdown or complete knockout. The CRISPRi experiments conducted by Baumgarten and colleagues were able to reduce expression, but not eliminate it [29]. An unannotated accessory protein, VIRMA (PF3D7_1366300) was identified with the METTL3-METTL14-WTAP writer complex in P. falciparum [62]. The unannotated VIRMA protein may be an effective target for the development of novel therapeutics that can diminish the ability of P. falciparum to deposit m6A modifications necessary for controlling gene expression and parasitic growth. However, further investigation into this unannotated accessory protein will be required to demonstrate its efficacy as a therapeutic target. In T. gondii, the METTL3 component of the m6A writer complex achieves a very different result. The depletion of auxin-inducible degron tagged METTL3 and WTAP by incubation with indole-3-acetic acid caused decreases in the levels of m6A modified mRNA transcripts [62]. Furthermore, METTL3 and WTAP depletion in T. gondii caused the cessation of parasite replication, making these components of the m6A writer complex attractive targets for new antiparasitic drugs [62]. The finding that T. gondii METTL3 and WTAP depletion raises questions about which chemical agents can be used to safely during infection to stop the parasitic replication.

Apicomplexan and kinetoplastid parasites lack known, conserved m6A modification erasers unlike in humans that have known demethylase erasers. The lack of known m6A erasers in protozoan parasites, suggests that this modification could be unidirectional in these parasites. If the m6A modification is irreversible in apicomplexans and kinetoplastids, it leaves these parasitic protozoa vulnerable to intentional epitranscriptomic manipulation of gene expression. Selective inhibition of the writers can change the gene expression program without disrupting the host demethylases and causing instability in the parasite’s transcriptome, and by extension, proteome. While this possible avenue for therapeutic development is appealing, it is of note that the lack of known eraser demethylases does not necessarily equate to there being no eraser demethylases at all-assuming that the eraser demethylases observed in later branching eukaryotes are the only method of reversing m6A modifications does not give consideration the possibility that these early-branching eukaryotes may have a completely different method of reversing m6A modifications that has not yet been uncovered.

m6A is a crucial epitranscriptomic modification that influences every part of the RNA life cycle. The full breadth of m6A functions is not currently known, but this modification has demonstrated roles in cellular localization of transcripts, alternative splicing, protein translation, transcript stabilization and degradation. While the identification of m6A modifications has improved by leaps and bounds over the last few decades, we still have quite a way to go in characterizing the impacts of these modifications on individual transcripts, especially in the protozoan parasites where very few m6A regulators are known so far. Recent findings suggest that non-canonical m6A methyl-readers may play significant roles in post-transcriptional gene regulation in parasitic protists. In T. brucei, TRRM2, a protein harboring an RNA recognition motif (RRM) has been identified as a potential m6A reader, expanding the landscape of m6A effectors beyond the well-known YTH domain family [80]. Likewise, P. falciparum encodes NOVA-1-like RNA-binding proteins (PlasmoDB) containing KH domains, which are structurally suited to recognize RNA modifications such as m6A [100]. These discoveries highlight the evolutionary adaptation of RNA-binding proteins with diverse domain architectures to interpret epitranscriptomic marks, underscoring the need for broader functional characterization of non-canonical m6A readers in protozoan pathogens The future of this field also relies on the integration of m6A modification identification with studies of m6A stoichiometry and interactions with other epitranscriptomic modifications to draw conclusions about the function of individual m6A modifications.
